newsitem.title: USA: US CREDIT OUTLOOK - Durable goods market's focus.
newsitem.headline: US CREDIT OUTLOOK - Durable goods market's focus.

text.p: The prices of U.S. Treasury securities were expected to tread tight ranges on Wednesday as few players were seen making large plays ahead of the central bank's policy-making meeting next week.

Durable goods orders were scheduled for release at 0830 EDT/1230 GMT. Economists surveyed by Reuters expected, on average, that goods would rise by 0.6 percent in May, lower than April's 1.3 percent, but a number indicative of continued strength. However, analysts warned, the number was highly volatile and subject to sharp revisions.
"There are two markets here -- the long end and the short end," said Hugh Johnson, chief economist at First Albany Corp.
Johnson said short-term bill rates were rising -- or losing value -- while long-term rates remained flat in recent sessions.

"It's one of two things. Either investors are worried the Federal Reserve will raise rates or are taking seriously (Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro) Hashimoto's statement that Japan would sell Treasuries," Johnson said.
While most analysts have dismissed the statement, Johnson said it did show the Japanese wanted the yen to stabilize.

"He's (Hashimoto) worried their economic pickup could lead to higher inflation at a time when they're trying to restore health to their banking system," Johnson said. "If you read between the lines, the rise in short-term interest rates says there is some contiguousness between Japan and the U.S. -- so don't dismiss his comments."
Three-month bills rose eight basis points at Monday's close following Hashimoto's comments.
Johnson said continuing rises in short-term interest rates would point to investors' belief that the second-quarter slowdown in economic growth was not just a pause.
Johnson said non-defense capital goods would be the most watched component of the durable goods report. The number usually was not a market mover, he added.
Also on the data calendar were existing homes sales, expected to have risen slightly to a 4.07 million annualized rate, up from 4.06 million in April.
The Wall Street dealer community also looked to absorb $11.5 billion in five-year notes following the auction of $15.0 billion in two-year notes on Tuesday.
Treasury also raised the size of its regular three- and six-month auctions on Tuesday by $1 billion to $15 billion.

Michael Strauss, chief economist at Sanwa Securities (USA) Co, expected to see problems with the durable goods report on Wednesday. He saw orders rising by 1.5 percent in the month, a figure in the high range of most economists' expectations.
"The risk is we'll see a stronger number (than consensus expectations) print," Strauss said. There could be problems with distribution of Treasury's five-year notes, he said.

"The Street is probably long a fair amount at these levels," Strauss said. Few expected the Fed to move next week, the question was whether growth began to resurface in the third quarter, he said. Strauss expected it would.
Late Tuesday, the Treasury's 30-year bond was trading at 99-3/32, up 4/32, to yield 6.70 percent.

At the short end of the maturity spectrum the three-month bill rate was up one basis point at 5.01 percent. Six-month bills were up one basis point at 5.08 percent and year-bills were down one basis point at 5.35 percent.
Five-year notes were up 1/32 at 100-26/32, yielding 6.30 percent. Ten-year notes were up 3/32 at 101-18/32, yielding 6.41 percent.
(N.A. Treasury Desk, 212-859-1663))
